title: Design backup and disaster recovery
learningObjective: Recommend recovery solutions for Azure and hybrid workloads that meet RPO and RTO, and backup and recovery for compute, databases and unstructured data.
foundation: Two numbers drive every recovery design. RPO (recovery point objective): how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. RTO (recovery time objective): how long you can be down.
Backup lets you go back in time (after a mistake or ransomware). Disaster recovery keeps the service running somewhere else (after a regional outage). Most systems need both.
Smaller RPO and RTO cost more, so set them per workload with the business.
engineer: Recovery design: classify workloads (mission-critical, business-critical, other) with RPO/RTO targets; choose backup, replication or active-active accordingly; document runbooks and test failovers regularly (Site Recovery test failover doesn't affect production). Use paired or chosen secondary regions; consider data residency.

Compute: Azure Backup for VMs (Standard policy: daily; Enhanced: every 4–24 hours, longer instant-restore snapshots, required for Trusted Launch in the portal), restore as new VM, replace disks or file-level recovery. Azure Site Recovery replicates Azure VMs to another region (and VMware, Hyper-V or physical servers to Azure) with crash-consistent recovery points every few minutes, app-consistent points on a schedule, recovery plans for multi-tier ordering, and test failovers. Hybrid: MARS agent for files and folders, Azure Backup Server or DPM for on-premises workloads.

Databases: Azure SQL automated backups with point-in-time restore (1–35 days), long-term retention (weekly, monthly, yearly up to 10 years), geo-restore from geo-redundant backups (RPO about 1 hour, RTO up to about 12 hours), active geo-replication (readable secondaries, RPO about 5 seconds) and auto-failover groups (listener endpoints, SQL Database and Managed Instance). SQL Server in VMs: Azure Backup with 15-minute log backups. Cosmos DB: continuous backup with point-in-time restore (7 or 30 days) or periodic backup.

Unstructured data: blob soft delete, versioning, point-in-time restore, operational and vaulted backup for blobs, object replication; Azure Files share snapshots and Azure Backup for Files (snapshot and vaulted tiers); geo-redundant storage with customer-managed failover. Protect backups: vault soft delete, immutable vaults, multi-user authorization with Resource Guard, and cross-region restore on GRS vaults.

example.title: RPO/RTO tiers for an insurer
body: Mission-critical claims system (RPO 5 minutes, RTO 1 hour): VMs replicated with Site Recovery to a second region, database in an auto-failover group, quarterly test failovers. Daily Enhanced-policy backups protect against corruption and ransomware.

Internal tools (RPO 24 hours, RTO 24 hours): daily Azure Backup only, with cross-region restore. Documents: versioning, soft delete and vaulted blob backup; yearly SQL long-term retention for 7 years.

prerequisites: An Azure subscription; most design reviews need only Reader access
permissions: Reader to review existing resources; Contributor or Owner to build the design
limits: Check service limits and regional availability for each component
portal: Recovery Services vault > Backup / Site Recovery: enable replication, recovery plans, test failover.
Backup vault > Backup policies (blobs, disks, PostgreSQL).
SQL server > Backups: retention policies, long-term retention; Failover groups.

troubleshooting.symptom: After ransomware, the DR copy is encrypted too.
troubleshooting.fix: Restore from point-in-time backups (protected with immutable vault and soft delete).

troubleshooting.symptom: The app can't connect after a SQL geo-failover.
troubleshooting.cause: Connection string points to the old primary server.
troubleshooting.fix: Use the failover group's listener endpoint.

comparisons.difference: Backup restores data to a point in time; Site Recovery fails whole workloads over to another region.
Geo-restore: cheap, hours of RTO and ~1 h RPO. Geo-replication: running secondary, seconds of RPO.

misconceptions.reality: It replicates corruption and deletions too.

misconceptions.myth: RTO is how much data you lose.
misconceptions.reality: That is RPO; RTO is downtime.

architectureDecisions: Backup for every workload; DR (Site Recovery, failover groups) for those that need it.
Protect backups: soft delete, immutability, Resource Guard; test restores and failovers.

walkthrough.subtitle: Lose as little data and as little time as the business can accept, and no more than it pays for.
learn: Recovery for files and blobs, and protecting backups

steps.label: Problem
steps.title: A region fails — or ransomware strikes
body: Different disasters need different answers. First agree two numbers with the business.

steps.label: Targets
steps.title: RPO and RTO
body: RPO: how much data you can lose (minutes? a day?). RTO: how long you can be down. Smaller numbers mean more cost, so set them per workload.

steps.label: Two tools
steps.title: Backup goes back in time; DR goes somewhere else
body: Backups recover from mistakes, corruption and ransomware. Disaster recovery replicates to another region so the service keeps running when a region fails.

callout.text: Replication copies ransomware damage too — you still need backups.

steps.label: Compute + data
steps.title: VMs and databases
body: VMs: Azure Backup plus Site Recovery for regional failover with test failovers. SQL: point-in-time restore (up to 35 days), long-term retention (up to 10 years), and failover groups for a geo-replica with seconds of RPO.

steps.label: Files + protection
steps.title: Blobs, files and safe backups
body: Blobs: soft delete, versioning, vaulted backup. Files: share snapshots and Azure Backup. Protect the backups themselves with soft delete, immutable vaults and Resource Guard.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: Recovery design
recap: VMs: Backup + Site Recovery; SQL: PITR, LTR, failover groups
Blobs/files: versioning, snapshots, vaulted backup; protect backups
